submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole is not a content detector but GPT-2's GELU dip read on neuron 2191's pre-activation z: the MLP activation is gelu_new, so the negative pole reads -min(gelu_new(z), 0), capped at 0.17004 (any z in about [-0.91, -0.60] reads within 3% of the cap), exactly 0 whenever z >= 0, and below the 0.25-of-scale activity line (0.0425) whenever z > -0.09 or z < about -2.0, with z set almost entirely by the current token's own layer-5 residual (82% of the input attribution is on the peak token, mean distance 0.7 tokens) and both vocabulary lenses flat (Jacobian kurtosis 2.83, 10% agreement), because the opposite pole is broadly active on ordinary English prose and leaves its zeros on the tokens where that key matches. Label a prompt ACTIVE when any measured token's z falls in that band and INACTIVE only when every token's does not: a one-token prompt is always INACTIVE whatever the token (at position 0 z is a fixed -0.011 to -0.066 across all 50,257 vocabulary tokens, peak strength <= 0.031, measured), running text is in the band at ~43% of its tokens (228/548 scanned; 0.427 over 20,405 tokens of the 500-document corpus.jsonl), so a 16-token span is active with probability ~0.99 and peaks at the cap with probability ~0.6 (0.74 at 24 tokens, and every one of the 40 documents I measured, 20,405 tokens, peaks within 3e-3 of the cap), and within running text which word lands in the band is not predictable from content: a one-word substitution inside a saturated passage leaves the peak at the cap, and only removing a span's single in-band token (e.g. 'The study ...' to 'The analysis ...') drops it.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The river rises in the uplands and runs east for about eighty miles before it reaches the plain. For most of its course it passes through farmland, where hedges divide the fields and small woods stand on the higher ground. In the nineteenth century mills were built along its banks, and although few of them still work, their brick walls and tall chimneys remain. The water is slow here, and in summer the surface is covered with weed and the leaves of water lilies. Boats are hired at the village quay, and visitors row upstream towards the old bridge, passing herons and the occasional kingfisher. Beyond the bridge the valley narrows and the current quickens, and the path climbs through beech woods to a ridge with views across three counties. Walkers often stop at the ruined chapel, where a stone altar and a few carved capitals survive. The chapel was abandoned in the sixteenth century, and its roof fell in long ago, so that the walls now enclose a rectangle of grass and nettles. Farmers graze sheep on the slopes above, and in autumn the woods turn brown and the fields are bare. A small museum in the village keeps maps, photographs and tools from the mills, and a retired engineer has written a short history of the river. His book describes the flood of eighteen seventy-five, when the bridge was damaged and the lower fields were under water for a week. Since then the banks have been raised in several places, and a weir was built to control the flow. The weir is still maintained, and on quiet evenings its sound carries across the meadows to the houses at the edge of the village. Beyond the village the river turns south and runs through a wide marsh, where reeds grow taller than a man and the water lies in shallow pools. Wildfowl gather there in winter, and birdwatchers come with telescopes and notebooks. The marsh drains slowly, and after heavy rain the footpath is often flooded, so walkers take the higher track through the wood. At the southern end of the marsh a sluice controls the outflow, and beyond it the river becomes tidal. The tide fills the channel twice a day, and at high water the mud banks disappear beneath a brown sheet that reflects the sky. Small boats lie at anchor near the harbour wall, and gulls follow the fishing boats in from the sea. The harbour itself is sheltered by a stone pier built in the eighteenth century, now patched with concrete and topped by a light that flashes at night. Fishermen mend nets on the quay, and a fish market stands at the top of the street.
